summary.text: The counterexample is $27$: for every $k\ge2$, $k^{27}-27=(k^9-3)(k^{18}+3k^9+9)$ has two factors greater than $1$, while $k=0,1$ cannot yield a positive prime, so no prime of the required form exists. Yet $27\equiv3\pmod4$, whereas every square of an even integer is divisible by $4$.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
S_n=\{p\in\mathbb N: p\text{ is prime and }k^n=p+n\text{ for some }k\in\mathbb N\}.
\]
The sequence value \(a(n)\) is the least element of \(S_n\), with the convention that \(a(n)=0\) when \(S_n\) is empty. We disprove the conjecture by taking \(n=27\). We will prove both that \(S_{27}\) is empty, so that \(a(27)=0\), and that \(27\) is not the square of an even integer.

First we show that no number of the form \(k^{27}-27\) can be prime. Suppose that \(p,k\in\mathbb N\) satisfy
\[
k^{27}=p+27.
\]
We divide into cases according to the size of \(k\).

If \(k<2\), then \(k=0\) or \(k=1\). For \(k=0\), the displayed equality would say
\[
0=0^{27}=p+27,
\]
which is impossible in the natural numbers because \(p+27\ge 27>0\). For \(k=1\), it would say
\[
1=1^{27}=p+27,
\]
which is likewise impossible because \(p+27\ge27>1\). Thus there are no solutions at all with \(k<2\).

It remains to consider \(k\ge2\). Put \(x=k^9\). Then
\[
k^{27}=x^3,\qquad k^{18}=x^2.
\]
The standard difference-of-cubes identity gives
\[
x^3-3^3=(x-3)(x^2+3x+9).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
k^{27}=(k^9-3)(k^{18}+3k^9+9)+27.
\]
Comparing this with \(k^{27}=p+27\) and subtracting \(27\) yields
\[
p=(k^9-3)(k^{18}+3k^9+9). \tag{1}
\]
This subtraction causes no issue in the natural numbers: since \(k\ge2\), we have \(k^9\ge2^9=512\), in particular \(k^9\ge3\), so all quantities in the factorization are nonnegative.

Both factors on the right side of (1) are greater than \(1\). Indeed,
\[
k^9-3\ge 2^9-3=509\ge2,
\]
and
\[
k^{18}+3k^9+9\ge9\ge2.
\]
Consequently (1) expresses \(p\) as a product of two natural numbers, each at least \(2\). Hence \(p\) is composite and therefore cannot be prime. More explicitly, the first factor \(k^9-3\) divides \(p\); it is not \(1\), and because the second factor is at least \(2\), it is strictly smaller than \(p\). Thus \(p\) has a nontrivial divisor, contradicting primality.

We have now covered every natural-number base \(k\): for \(k=0,1\), the equation \(k^{27}=p+27\) has no natural-number solution \(p\), while for every \(k\ge2\), any resulting value \(p=k^{27}-27\) factors nontrivially and is not prime. Therefore there is no prime \(p\) and no \(k\in\mathbb N\) satisfying
\[
k^{27}=p+27.
\]
In other words, \(S_{27}=\varnothing\). By the defining convention for the sequence, this proves
\[
a(27)=0.
\]

Finally, \(27\) is not the square of an even integer. If there were an \(m\in\mathbb N\) such that
\[
27=(2m)^2,
\]
then
\[
27=4m^2.
\]
The right side is divisible by \(4\), so it is congruent to \(0\pmod4\), whereas
\[
27\equiv3\pmod4.
\]
This is impossible. Hence there is no \(m\in\mathbb N\) with \(27=(2m)^2\).

Thus \(k=27\) is an index for which \(a(k)=0\), but \(k\) is not the square of an even integer. This counterexample disproves the conjecture.
